arXiv:2507.00683v1 [cond-mat.mtrl-sci] 01 Jul 2025

Testing the spin-bath view of self-attention: A Hamiltonian analysis of GPT-2 Transformer

Satadeep Bhattacharjee1 Email: s.bhattacharjee@ikst.res.in Affiliation: 1 Indo-Korea Science and Technology Center (IKST), Bangalore, India
2 Electronic Materials Research Center, Korea Institute of Science &\& Technology, Korea    Seung-Cheol Lee2 Affiliation: 1 Indo-Korea Science and Technology Center (IKST), Bangalore, India
2 Electronic Materials Research Center, Korea Institute of Science &\& Technology, Korea
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The recently proposed physics-based framework by Huo and Johnson [1] models the attention mechanism of Large Language Models (LLMs) as an interacting two-body spin system, offering a first-principles explanation for phenomena like repetition and bias. Building on this hypothesis, we extract the complete Query-Key weight matrices from a production-grade GPT-2 model and derive the corresponding effective Hamiltonian for every attention head. From these Hamiltonians we obtain analytic phase boundaries logit gap criteria that predict which token should dominate the next-token distribution for a given context. A systematic evaluation on 144 heads across 20 factual-recall prompts reveals a strong negative correlation between the theoretical logit gaps and the model’s empirical token rankings (r≈−0.70r\approx-0.70, p<10−3p<10^{-3}). Targeted ablations further show that suppressing the heads most aligned with the spin-bath predictions induces the anticipated shifts in output probabilities, confirming a causal link rather than a coincidental association. Taken together, our findings provide the first strong empirical evidence for the spin-bath analogy in a production-grade model. This validation not only furnishes a tractable, physics-inspired lens for interpretability but also provides the groundwork for novel generative models, bridging the gap between theoretical condensed matter physics and AI.

I Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc. have revolutionized natural language processing by achieving human-level performance on tasks ranging from text generation to translation. Beyond their usual uses, in recent past, it has been seen that autoregressive LLM pipelines can not only write reliable chemical sequences for materials for energy storage [2], but also generate plausible crystal structures [3, 4] whose ab initio stability tests rival conventional materials design workflows, suggesting that linguistic priors can encode latent chemical grammar. Yet their decision-making processes remain opaque and difficult to interpret [5, 6, 7]. Recent work by Huo and Johnson [1] offers a compelling theoretical lens, casting the Transformer’s Query–Key attention mechanism as a classical two-body spin Hamiltonian. In this picture, each token embedding plays the role of a spin vector, and the learned Query–Key weight matrix WeffW_{\mathrm{eff}} defines effective exchange interactions that, through a soft-max Boltzmann distribution, determine the probability of selecting one token over another. This analogy not only recovers familiar pathologies—such as repetition loops and bias amplification—as phase-transition phenomena in an effective spin bath, but also suggests a rich toolkit of statistical-mechanics methods for probing model behavior [8].

It is worth noting that connecting the attention mechanism to the spin Hamiltonians is not a new trend. It was postulated earlier by Rende et al., who showed that when the positional and embedding sub-spaces are decoupled, a single self-attention layer is exactly equivalent to learning the conditional probabilities of a generalized Potts model [9, 10]. Li et al. [11] map a single-layer linear Transformer to a dense real-valued spin-glass Hamiltonian.

Despite its elegance, the spin-bath framework has thus far been illustrated only on toy examples, leaving its applicability to real, large-scale models untested. In this work, we provide a first rigorous experimental test of the spin-bath framework on a production-grade model: Generative Pre-trained Transformer version 2. We performed the token generation using the GPT-2 transformer model using the Huggingface Transformers library [12, 13]. By isolating the Query–Key sub-matrices of GPT–2, we construct the effective two-body Hamiltonian head-by-head and derive closed-form predictions for logit-gap “phase boundaries” between candidate tokens. Using a diverse factual-recall benchmark we show:

  1. 1.

    A statistically significant correlation between logit gaps obtained from the Hamiltonian and the actual next-token preferences across 144 heads and 20 prompts, with a single head from a pretrained GPT-2 model.

  2. 2.

    Geometric visualisation of this head’s decision boundary reveals antagonistic behaviour consistent with a mean-field context field, directly corroborating spin-bath predictions.

  3. 3.

    Causal ablation confirms that the identified heads exert the predicted directional influence on model output, establishing that the correlations are not merely epiphenomenal.

These findings connect the recent theoretical developments and practical LLM interpretability. This work demonstrates that much of GPT–2’s token selection can indeed be understood as the energetics of pairwise spin interactions, while simultaneously situating our results within the broader Potts-model. By validating a tractable two-body description in situ, our study opens the way for importing equilibrium and non-equilibrium techniques—temperature scaling, disorder perturbations, finite-size analysis—into the toolkit of mechanistic interpretability and for developing physics-inspired interventions that are both mathematically grounded and empirically verified.

II Theoretical Framework and Methodology

Our study adopts the theoretical formulation introduced by Huo and Johnson [1], which recasts the self-attention mechanism of Transformer models as a two-body spin Hamiltonian. In a classical Heisenberg magnet, the two-body interaction energy is given by

HHeis=−∑i<jJi​j𝐒i⋅𝐒j,H_{\mathrm{Heis}}\;=\;-\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\,\mathbf{S}_{i}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}_{j},

where Ji​jJ_{ij} is the microscopic exchange coupling—positive Ji​jJ_{ij} favors ferromagnetic alignment of spins 𝐒i\mathbf{S}_{i} and 𝐒j\mathbf{S}_{j}, while negative Ji​jJ_{ij} favors antiferromagnetic order. In the spin–bath analogy for self-attention this exchange tensor is replaced by the learned Query–Key coupling matrix

Weff=WQ​WK⊤dhead,W_{\mathrm{eff}}\;=\;\frac{W_{Q}\,W_{K}^{\!\top}}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}},

so that the corresponding two-body “attention Hamiltonian” reads

H(0)​(Sj,Si)=−Sj​Weff​Si⊤.H^{(0)}(S_{j},S_{i})\;=\;-\,S_{j}\,W_{\mathrm{eff}}\,S_{i}^{\!\top}.

Here, WQW_{Q} and WKW_{K} are the learned query and key projection matrices for a given attention head, and dheadd_{\mathrm{head}} is the dimensionality of these internal query and key vectors. In this formulation, each attention head behaves like a spin-coupled system, with the predicted preference for a candidate token determined by the alignment of its key-space projection with an effective context field. The central theoretical object is the so-called Context Vector N(0)N^{(0)}, which summarizes the head’s aggregated preference from earlier tokens. Although Ji​jJ_{ij} originates from orbital overlaps or superexchange processes in a real material and WeffW_{\mathrm{eff}} is fit to linguistic data during pre-training, both tensors occupy the identical mathematical role of weighting the dot-product of two unit spins. Consequently, each element (Weff)i​j(W_{\mathrm{eff}})_{ij} quantifies an effective “semantic exchange” strength in direct analogy to the magnetic exchange Ji​jJ_{ij}, and the eigenmodes of WeffW_{\mathrm{eff}} reveal principal collective semantics just as diagonalization of Ji​jJ_{ij} yields magnon eigenmodes in a solid. The purpose of our work is to test this prediction directly in the pretrained GPT-2 small model [6], moving beyond illustrative examples to a quantitative validation using statistical and causal tools. Our approach isolates the Query–Key interactions from the Value pathway to rigorously assess how well the two-body spin Hamiltonian captures next-token preferences.

II.1 Theoretical Logit Difference from a Single Head’s Output

To isolate and quantify the contribution of a single attention head to the final next-token decision, we compute a theoretical logit difference, Δ​Ltheory\Delta L_{\text{theory}}, derived from that head’s complete output. This approach allows us to model the head’s influence as it is passed to the next stage of the Transformer (either the feed-forward network or the next layer).

We begin with an input prompt comprising kk tokens. Their embeddings, drawn from the token embedding matrix WEW_{E}, form a matrix 𝐗∈ℝk×dmodel\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d_{\text{model}}}. For a single attention head hh, its computation involves three learned projection matrices: Query WQ(h)W_{Q}^{(h)}, Key WK(h)W_{K}^{(h)}, and Value WV(h)W_{V}^{(h)}, all in ℝdmodel×dhead\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{head}}}. The embeddings are projected into these lower-dimensional subspaces:

Q=𝐗​WQ(h),K=𝐗​WK(h),V=𝐗​WV(h).Q=\mathbf{X}W_{Q}^{(h)},\quad K=\mathbf{X}W_{K}^{(h)},\quad V=\mathbf{X}W_{V}^{(h)}.

For the final token in the prompt (at position kk), its query vector QkQ_{k} interacts with all key vectors KjK_{j} in the context to compute attention scores, scaled by τ=dhead\tau=\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}:

Ωj=Qk⋅Kjτ.\Omega_{j}=\frac{Q_{k}\cdot K_{j}}{\tau}.

These scores are converted into attention weights αj\alpha_{j} via a softmax function, αj=softmax​(Ωj)\alpha_{j}=\text{softmax}(\Omega_{j}).

From a physics perspective, these weights determine how information from different "spin" states (context tokens) is averaged. The head’s primary output is a context vector, 𝐍0(h)\mathbf{N}_{0}^{(h)}, formed by the weighted sum of Value vectors. This vector represents the information aggregated by the head from the prompt context.

𝐍0(h)=∑j=1kαj​Vj.\mathbf{N}_{0}^{(h)}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\alpha_{j}V_{j}. (1)

This context vector 𝐍0(h)\mathbf{N}_{0}^{(h)} resides in the head’s value-space (dimension dheadd_{\text{head}}). To be integrated back into the model’s main computational pathway (the residual stream), it is projected back to the full model dimension by a learned output matrix WO(h)∈ℝdmodel×dheadW_{O}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{head}}}:

𝐍proj(h)=𝐍0(h)​(WO(h))⊤.\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}^{(h)}=\mathbf{N}_{0}^{(h)}(W_{O}^{(h)})^{\top}. (2)

The vector 𝐍proj(h)\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}^{(h)} represents the complete output of the attention head—the "message" it contributes to the model’s ongoing representation of the context.

To predict the head’s preference for the next token, we assume this projected context vector acts as an effective field on the full vocabulary. The theoretical logit for any candidate next token (e.g., token AA) is modeled as the alignment between the head’s output and the token’s own embedding, SA∈ℝ1×dmodelS_{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{\text{model}}}, drawn from the same matrix WEW_{E}.

Ltheory(A)=𝐍proj(h)⋅SA⊤.L_{\text{theory}}^{(A)}=\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}^{(h)}\cdot S_{A}^{\top}.

The theoretical logit difference between two candidate tokens, AA and BB, is therefore:

Δ​Ltheory=Ltheory(A)−Ltheory(B)=𝐍proj(h)⋅(SA−SB)⊤.\Delta L_{\text{theory}}=L_{\text{theory}}^{(A)}-L_{\text{theory}}^{(B)}=\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}^{(h)}\cdot(S_{A}-S_{B})^{\top}. (3)

This formulation captures the head’s full Q-K-V-O pathway and provides a direct, quantitative prediction of its influence on the final logit difference.

II.2 Logit Differences as physically meaningful metrics

In Transformer models, each token is assigned a scalar logit Li∈ℝL_{i}\in\mathbb{R}, which serves as an unnormalized score reflecting the model’s preference for that token in the given context. These logits are passed through a soft-max function to produce normalized probabilities:

Pi=eLi/τZ,Z=∑j∈𝒱eLj/τ,P_{i}=\frac{e^{L_{i}/\tau}}{Z},\qquad Z=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{V}}e^{L_{j}/\tau},

where 𝒱\mathcal{V} denotes the vocabulary and τ=dhead\tau=\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}} serves as an effective temperature. From a statistical-physics perspective, this normalization constant ZZ plays the role of a partition function, and each logit corresponds to minus the energy of a token: Ei=−LiE_{i}=-L_{i}. Hence, the soft-max implements a Boltzmann distribution over candidate tokens.

In this setting, the logit difference between two tokens,

Δ​L=Lgood−Lbad,\Delta L=L_{\text{good}}-L_{\text{bad}},

directly sets the energy gap Δ​E=−Δ​L\Delta E=-\Delta L and determines their relative odds via the exponential relation:

PgoodPbad=eΔ​L/τ.\frac{P_{\text{good}}}{P_{\text{bad}}}=e^{\Delta L/\tau}.

This quantity is particularly well-suited for comparing theoretical predictions with actual model behavior for several reasons. First, Δ​L\Delta L is invariant under any additive offset to all logits, such as those introduced by residual connections or layer normalizations. Second, it is independent of the absolute value of the partition function ZZ, which may vary unpredictably across prompts. Third, Δ​L\Delta L remains valid under changes in temperature, entering as a linear scaling in exp⁡(Δ​L/τ)\exp(\Delta L/\tau).

Throughout this study, we adopt Δ​L\Delta L as the primary metric of comparison between the theoretical two-body model and GPT-2’s empirical next-token preferences. This choice captures the model’s decision boundary in a form that is physically interpretable, statistically robust, and directly comparable to the Hamiltonian’s energy gap.

III Experimental Procedure

Our multi-stage validation uses this calculation as its core. The procedure is as follows:

  1. 1.

    Systematic Validation Dataset: We constructed a dataset of 20 diverse factual-recall prompts (see Appendix A for the complete prompt list). For each prompt, we defined a correct "good" token and an incorrect "bad" token.

  2. 2.

    Statistical Correlation Analysis: We calculated Δ​Ltheory\Delta L_{\text{theory}} for all 144 heads on all 20 prompts. We compared this to the empirical logit difference, Δ​Lactual\Delta L_{\text{actual}}, from the full model’s output. We performed a linear regression analysis to identify the most consistently predictive heads and to quantify the statistical significance of their correlation.

  3. 3.

    Causal Ablation: To test for causality, we used PyTorch hooks to perform head ablation on a representative prompt. By zeroing out a head’s contribution during the forward pass, we measured the resulting change in the final model’s output, allowing us to distinguish correlational from causal effects.

IV Results and Discussion.

Our empirical validation of the spin-bath model proceeded in three stages: a systematic, statistical analysis to identify functionally relevant attention heads; a mechanistic visualization of a key head’s decision geometry; and a causal intervention to confirm its role.

IV.1 Statistical Identification of a Predictive Head

To move beyond single-prompt anecdotes, we first tested the predictive power of all 144 heads in GPT-2 across a diverse dataset of 20 factual recall prompts. For each head, we computed the Pearson correlation between its theoretically-predicted logit difference (Δ​Ltheory\Delta L_{\text{theory}}) and the final logit difference of the full model (Δ​Lactual\Delta L_{\text{actual}}).

This systematic search identified Layer 3, Head 5 (L3H5) as the most consistently predictive component. The results, plotted in Figure 1, reveal a strong and statistically significant negative correlation (r≈−0.70r\approx-0.70, p<0.001p<0.001). A linear regression yields a coefficient of determination of r2∼0.48r^{2}\sim 0.48, indicating that the simple 2-body model for this single head can account for over 48% of the variance in the final output of the entire 12-layer model on this task set. This establishes L3H5 as a head with a significant and consistently antagonistic function—it reliably pushes against the correct answer when the model as a whole favors it. This finding highlights the ability of the physics framework to uncover non-obvious functional roles within the network.

To mechanistically dissect the statistical antagonism of Head L3H5, Fig. 2 visualizes the head’s decision-making process within its internal value space. The plot is oriented along two principal axes: the vertical “Decision Axis” (Δ​S=Sgood−Sbad\Delta S=S_{\text{good}}-S_{\text{bad}}) and a horizontal orthogonal axis. The background colormap represents the head’s internal preference field, determined by the alignment with its output Context Vector (𝐍0\mathbf{N}_{0}, shown as a black arrow); red regions are favorable to the head, while blue regions are unfavorable.

The figure reveals a sophisticated, two-step computational mechanism. For the prompt “The capital of Germany is…,” the correct continuation “Berlin” (green circle) is located deep within the favorable-red-region. This demonstrates that the head’s primary QK-V mechanism acts as a competent feature detector, correctly identifying that “Berlin” is semantically aligned with what should come next.

This presents a seeming contradiction: if the head internally favors the correct token, why does it have a strong antagonistic correlation with the model’s final output? The resolution lies in the second step of the attention mechanism, where the head’s output 𝐍0\mathbf{N}_{0} is projected back to the residual stream via its output matrix, 𝐖O\mathbf{W}_{O}. The final, calculated logit contribution of this head for this prompt is -0.1950. This negative value confirms that the 𝐖O\mathbf{W}_{O} matrix for L3H5 is structured to invert the head’s internally correct preference.

IV.2 Influence of global generation temperature on output Order

Beyond the effective internal temperature τhead=dhead\tau_{\text{head}}=\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}} that scales dot products within individual attention heads (as discussed in Section II, the final token selection process in LLMs is critically influenced by an externally applied global generation temperature, denoted TT. This parameter scales the raw output logits, Lv∈ℝL_{v}\in\mathbb{R} for each token vv in the vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}, before the final softmax layer. The probability PvP_{v} of generating token vv is then given by the Boltzmann distribution:

Pv​(T)=exp⁡(Lv/T)∑j∈𝒱exp⁡(Lj/T).P_{v}(T)=\frac{\exp(L_{v}/T)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(L_{j}/T)}. (4)

This temperature TT thereby controls the stochasticity of the output. To characterize this global effect using physics-inspired metrics, we investigated the model’s output distribution as a function of TT. We performed a temperature sweep from T=0.1T=0.1 to T=2.5T=2.5 for the GPT-2 model across our factual-recall prompt set. Two key order parameters were tracked: the average Shannon entropy of the next-token probability distribution, S⁡(P⁡(T))S(P(T)), and the average probability of the most likely next token, Ptop-1​(T)P_{\text{top-1}}(T).

The Shannon entropy, a measure of the uncertainty or "disorder" in the probability distribution, was calculated as:

S(P(T))=−∑v∈𝒱Pv(T)log2Pv(T),S(P(T))=-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}P_{v}(T)\log_{2}P_{v}(T), (5)

where the logarithm is base 2, so entropy is measured in bits. The probability of the top-1 token, Ptop-1​(T)P_{\text{top-1}}(T), which quantifies the model’s confidence in its most preferred prediction, was determined by:

Ptop-1​(T)=maxv∈𝒱⁡{Pv​(T)}.P_{\text{top-1}}(T)=\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\{P_{v}(T)\}. (6)

These metrics were averaged over all prompts for each value of TT.

As depicted in Figure 3, the average next-token entropy S⁡(P⁡(T))S(P(T)) exhibited a monotonic increase with temperature. At low temperatures (T≈0.1T\approx 0.1), entropy was minimal (≈0.2\approx 0.2 bits), signifying a highly deterministic output distribution, analogous to a physical system in a low-energy, ordered state. As TT increased, entropy rose towards approximately 14 bits at T=2.5T=2.5, indicating a significantly more stochastic and diverse output, akin to a system exploring a larger volume of its phase space at higher thermal energies. Conversely, Ptop-1​(T)P_{\text{top-1}}(T) displayed an inverse relationship with temperature, starting near 0.95 at low TT and decreasing to approximately 0.02 at high TT. This behavior is characteristic of an order parameter, such as magnetization, which diminishes as thermal fluctuations disrupt long-range order in a system. Both parameters showed smooth, continuous changes, indicating a gradual transition from a deterministic to a more random generation regime, rather than a sharp phase transition. A notable crossover region was observed around T≈0.7−1.2T\approx 0.7-1.2, where the rate of change for both metrics began to moderate. These results empirically validate that the global generation temperature TT acts as an effective control mechanism, directly analogous to thermodynamic temperature in physical systems, governing the balance between exploitation of learned patterns and exploration of the output space. This global perspective on output stochasticity complements the head-specific analysis of the spin-bath model.

IV.3 Causal Role of Attention Heads

Having established a strong correlation, we next performed causal interventions to probe the system’s dynamics. We selected a prompt where the baseline model already exhibits an incorrect preference: for “Lions are carnivores. Cows are…”, the model incorrectly favors ‘omnivores‘ over ‘herbivores‘, yielding a negative logit difference (Δ​Lactual=−0.85\Delta L_{\text{actual}}=-0.85). We then performed head ablation using PyTorch hooks to measure the change in this output [14].

The results, shown in Figure 4, are revealing. First, ablating the antagonistic head L3H5 had a minimal causal impact on this specific prompt, shifting the logit difference only slightly to -0.88. This suggests that while L3H5 is statistically important across many contexts, its influence can be minor on a case-by-case basis, overshadowed by a coalition of other heads.

More strikingly, when we ablated a control head, L0H0, which had low predictive correlation overall, the model’s performance on this prompt degraded significantly, with the logit difference dropping to -1.72. This intervention uncovered a "hidden" function: for this particular context, L0H0 was a key task-aligned component, and its removal exposed the model’s underlying difficulty with the prompt.

These causal experiments demonstrate that model behavior is not dictated by single components but emerges from a complex, context-dependent interplay of many heads with both cooperative and antagonistic roles. The final decision is a systemic property, which our methodology successfully probes.

By demonstrating that self-attention in GPT-2 admits an exact mapping onto a two-body spin Hamiltonian—and by validating this mapping both statistically and causally—this study provides the NLP community with a principled, physics-inspired toolkit for interpretability. First, the logit-gap criteria derived from the Hamiltonian give a quantitative lens for ranking head importance that complements purely data-driven metrics. Second, the phase-boundary perspective invites the import of equilibrium and non-equilibrium techniques (e.g. temperature scaling, finite-size scaling) to probe robustness, calibration, and failure modes of attention mechanisms. Finally, by pinpointing both antagonistic and cooperative heads in situ, practitioners gain a mechanistically grounded route to targeted interventions—whether pruning for efficiency, editing to remove undesirable behaviors, or bias-mitigation through controlled perturbations—thus bridging the gap between empirical NLP engineering and theoretical foundations.

V Beyond Brownian Diffusion: Spin-dynamical generative models

The static, energetic perspective of the spin-bath model, while powerful for interpreting existing architectures, also suggests a profound extension towards novel, dynamically-evolving generative frameworks. In the following, we can argue that the spin–bath analogy discussed so far is not merely interpretative: it can inspire dynamical generative schemes whose core mathematics—spin precession plus viscous damping—surpasses the simplicity of Brownian drift–diffusion in standard score-based models.

V.1 From Static Hamiltonian to Dynamical Semantics

Our two-body attention Hamiltonian,

H(0)​(Sj,Si)=−Sj​Weff​Si⊤,H^{(0)}(S_{j},S_{i})\;=\;-\,S_{j}\,W_{\mathrm{eff}}\,S_{i}^{\!\top},

has until now offered a purely energetic interpretation of self-attention. In micromagnetics, however, the same Hamiltonian yields an effective field,

𝐁eff=−∂H∂𝐒,\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{eff}}\;=\;-\,\frac{\partial H}{\partial\mathbf{S}},

which drives the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert (LLG) dynamics of a spin [15]. By analogy, the context-aggregated value vector 𝐍proj\mathbf{N}_{\mathrm{proj}} (i.e. V​softmax​(Q​K⊤/d)V\,\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\!\top}/\sqrt{d})) plays the role of an internal field derived from the prompt.

V.2 LLG evolution of a token spin

We let a latent token spin 𝐒⁡(t)∈ℝd\mathbf{S}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} evolve under the internal field 𝐍proj\mathbf{N}_{\mathrm{proj}} while being buffeted by a thermal field 𝐡⁡(t)\mathbf{h}(t), i.e. the stochastic Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation [16],

𝐒˙=−γ𝐒×(𝐍proj+𝐡(t))−γλ1+λ2𝐒×[𝐒×(𝐍proj+𝐡(t))],\dot{\mathbf{S}}=-\gamma\,\mathbf{S}\times\!\bigl(\mathbf{N}_{\!\text{proj}}+\mathbf{h}(t)\bigr)-\gamma\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^{2}}\,\mathbf{S}\times\!\bigl[\mathbf{S}\times(\mathbf{N}_{\!\text{proj}}+\mathbf{h}(t))\bigr], (7)

with ⟨hα​(t)​hβ​(0)⟩=2​λ​kB​T​δα​β​δ​(t)\langle h_{\alpha}(t)h_{\beta}(0)\rangle=2\lambda k_{B}T\,\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta(t). The first cross product drives conservative precession, the second provides viscous damping, and the white-noise torque supplies exploration. Setting λ→∞\lambda\!\to\!\infty and linearising yields the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck forward process of Eq. (8), while 𝐡≡0\mathbf{h}\!\equiv\!0 reduces (7) to the usual deterministic form [15].

V.3 Contrast with Brownian Diffusion Models

Standard generative models like Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) realize text synthesis via Brownian drift–diffusion, governed by the stochastic differential equation [17, 18],

d​𝐱=fθ​(𝐱,t)​d​t+σ⁡(t)​d​𝐖td\mathbf{x}=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t)\,dt+\sigma(t)\,d\mathbf{W}_{t}

In this framework, the state variable 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a vector in unconstrained Euclidean space. The entire drift function fθf_{\theta} is a "black-box" neural network that must be learned from scratch, and the noise is a simple additive kick.

In stark contrast, our spin-dynamical formulation is built upon the physically-grounded stochastic Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert (LLG) equation. Here, a token’s latent representation is a unit-norm spin vector 𝐒\mathbf{S}, which evolves under the influence of the deterministic context field 𝐍proj\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}} and a stochastic thermal field 𝐡⁡(t)\mathbf{h}(t):

𝐒˙=−γ𝐒×(𝐍proj+𝐡(t))−γλ1+λ2𝐒×[𝐒×(𝐍proj+𝐡(t))]\dot{\mathbf{S}}=-\gamma\,\mathbf{S}\times\bigl(\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}+\mathbf{h}(t)\bigr)-\gamma\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^{2}}\,\mathbf{S}\times\bigl[\mathbf{S}\times(\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}+\mathbf{h}(t))\bigr]

To compare this directly with the Brownian model, we can separate the deterministic and stochastic parts. The deterministic drift is generated by 𝐍proj\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}, while the stochastic field 𝐡⁡(t)\mathbf{h}(t)-representing thermal fluctuations-gives rise to the diffusion term. This leads to the following SDE form:

d​𝐒=(−γ𝐒×𝐍proj−γλ1+λ2𝐒×[𝐒×𝐍proj])dt⏟Analytic, Structured Drift+(…)​d​𝐖t⏟Geometric Noised\mathbf{S}=\underbrace{\left(-\gamma\,\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}-\gamma\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^{2}}\,\mathbf{S}\times\left[\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}\right]\right)dt}_{\text{Analytic, Structured Drift}}+\underbrace{\left(\dots\right)d\mathbf{W}_{t}}_{\text{Geometric Noise}}

where the noise term on the right is derived directly from the torques created by 𝐡⁡(t)\mathbf{h}(t). This approach fundamentally differs from the Brownian model:

  1. 1.

    Structured Analytic Drift: The drift is not a monolithic learned function. It is decomposed into two physically meaningful components:

    • •

      Conservative Precession (−γ𝐒×𝐍proj-\gamma\,\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}): This term forces the spin 𝐒\mathbf{S} to rotate or "orbit" around the context field 𝐍proj\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}}. This provides a natural mechanism for exploring semantically adjacent concepts.

    • •

      Dissipative Damping (the second term): This term provides a torque that steers the spin towards alignment with the context field, forcing convergence to a low-energy (high-probability) state.

  2. 2.

    Reframed Learning Objective: Because the primary dynamics are analytic, the model inherits a powerful inductive bias. The neural network no longer needs to discover the entire vector field; it only needs to learn a residual correction to the known physical drift, or to the field 𝐍proj\mathbf{N}_{\text{proj}} itself. The bulk of the token–token physics is already encoded.

  3. 3.

    Inherent Geometric Constraint: The entire LLG dynamics, both drift and diffusion, is intrinsically defined on the unit sphere. The cross-product structure ensures that all motion, whether from the deterministic field or the stochastic noise, is tangential to the sphere. This naturally preserves the unit norm of the spin vector 𝐒\mathbf{S}, eliminating the need for ad-hoc projection steps.

Finally, the combination of conservative rotation and dissipative relaxation makes the LLG flow intrinsically non-reversible. Such dynamics are known to mix faster and escape local minima more efficiently than standard reversible Langevin dynamics, potentially leading to higher-quality samples with fewer generation steps. In this respect, the spin framework provides a more principled and structured alternative to conventional score-based models, replacing a black-box drifter with a rich, geometrically-aware dynamic.

V.4 Spin–diffusion blueprint

Forward (noising) process:

Training begins by corrupting every clean spin vector 𝐒0∈Sd−1\mathbf{S}_{0}\in S^{d-1} with an isotropic Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) dynamics that preserves spin length,

d​𝐒t=−β⁡(t)2​𝐒t​d​t+β⁡(t)​𝐏𝐒t∘d​𝐖t,d\mathbf{S}_{t}\;=\;-\tfrac{\beta(t)}{2}\,\mathbf{S}_{t}\,dt\;+\;\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}_{t}}\!\circ d\mathbf{W}_{t}, (8)

where 𝐏𝐒=𝐈−𝐒𝐒⊤\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{S}\mathbf{S}^{\!\top} projects to the tangent plane, d​𝐖td\mathbf{W}_{t} is a dd-dimensional Wiener increment, and β⁡(t)∈[0,βmax]\beta(t)\!\in[0,\beta_{\max}] is a monotonically increasing noise schedule. Equation (8) gradually drives the spin distribution toward the uniform measure on the sphere while erasing semantic information, exactly mirroring the Gaussian diffusion xt=α¯t​x0+1−α¯t​εx_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,x_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\varepsilon used in DDPMs. Because 𝐍proj\mathbf{N}_{\!\text{proj}} is absent during this phase, the forward corruption is Markov and fully tractable; the model learns to predict the time-dependent score ∇𝐒​log​qt​(𝐒t)\nabla_{\!\mathbf{S}}\!\log q_{t}(\mathbf{S}_{t}) from pairs (𝐒0,𝐒t)(\mathbf{S}_{0},\mathbf{S}_{t}) generated by (8).

Reverse (denoising / generation) process:

At sampling time we integrate the time-reversed SDE

d​𝐒t=[β⁡(t)2​𝐒t+β⁡(t)​(η​𝐍proj+∇𝐒​log​qtres)]​d​t+β⁡(t)​𝐏𝐒t∘d​𝐖¯t,d\mathbf{S}_{t}\;=\;\Bigl[\tfrac{\beta(t)}{2}\mathbf{S}_{t}+\beta(t)\bigl(\eta\,\mathbf{N}_{\!\text{proj}}+\nabla_{\!\mathbf{S}}\log q_{t}^{\mathrm{res}}\bigr)\Bigr]dt\;+\;\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{S}_{t}}\!\circ d\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t}, (9)

where a fixed scale factor η∈[0,1]\eta\!\in[0,1] reinstates the internal field 𝐍proj\mathbf{N}_{\!\text{proj}} and the residual score ∇𝐒​log​qtres\nabla_{\!\mathbf{S}}\log q_{t}^{\mathrm{res}} is supplied by the neural network. Rewriting (9) in the standard micromagnetic form exhibits a stochastic Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation with precession rate γ=η​β​(t)\gamma\!=\!\eta\,\beta(t), dimensionless damping α=1\alpha\!=\!1, and thermal-noise amplitude D⁡(t)=12​β​(t)D(t)=\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t): 𝐒˙=−γ𝐒×𝐍proj+α𝐒×𝐒˙+2​D​(t)𝜼(t).\dot{\mathbf{S}}=-\gamma\,\mathbf{S}\times\mathbf{N}_{\!\text{proj}}+\alpha\,\mathbf{S}\times\dot{\mathbf{S}}+\sqrt{2D(t)}\,\bm{\eta}(t). Starting from a maximally noisy spin 𝐒T∼qT\mathbf{S}_{T}\!\sim\!q_{T}, Euler–Maruyama steps of (9) progressively damp the noise while the precessional drift steers 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} towards regions preferred by the language model. When the schedule reaches t≈0t\!\approx\!0 the spin settles; a nearest-neighbour lookup in embedding space then yields the next token, which is appended to the context, 𝐍proj\mathbf{N}_{\!\text{proj}} is recomputed, and the diffusion chain is run again for the subsequent position.

V.5 Challenges and future directions

Drift–noise calibration.

The deterministic drift contains a fixed analytic field η​𝐍proj\eta\,\mathbf{N}_{\mathrm{proj}} and a tunable damping coefficient λ\lambda, while the stochastic kick has variance σ2​(t)\sigma^{2}(t). Incorrect relative scaling can overdamp the token spin or, conversely, leave it wandering. A principled schedule for (η,λ,σ)(\eta,\lambda,\sigma) is therefore essential.

Integrator stability.

Time–stepping a stochastic LLG on the unit hypersphere requires schemes that conserve |𝐒⁡(t)|=1|\mathbf{S}(t)|=1 and handle white-noise torques. Spin-preserving midpoint or symplectic integrators from micromagnetics, augmented with a projection step, are promising options.

Training objective.

The score can be split into an analytic part η​𝐍proj\eta\,\mathbf{N}_{\mathrm{proj}} and a learned residual fθf_{\theta}. The residual is trained with the standard DDPM noise-prediction loss, while η\eta can be annealed or learned by meta-gradient.

Empirical validation.

It remains to be tested whether injecting a physics-informed drift improves perplexity, sample diversity, or controllability compared with a purely learned score field. Ablation over (η,λ)(\eta,\lambda) and comparison to Brownian DDPM baselines will provide a decisive benchmark.

In summary, recasting language generation as spin-dynamical evolution under a self-generated field not only enriches the theoretical landscape—bridging magnetisation dynamics and generative AI—but also offers new inductive biases and control knobs for building next-generation diffusion-style models.

VI Conclusion

In this work, we demonstrated that applying the spin–bath Hamiltonian directly to the Query–Key weights of a production-scale Transformer enables quantitatively accurate and falsifiable predictions regarding the behavior of large language models. Our analysis across a diverse set of factual-recall tasks established a strong correlation between analytically computed logit gaps derived from the two-body Hamiltonian and empirically measured gaps, identifying Layer 3 Head 5 as a notably influential unit. Phase-boundary visualizations confirmed this head’s contrarian role—actively diverting probability from correct completions—while causal ablations revealed the model’s final outputs as arising from intricate competition among cooperative and antagonistic components. The efficacy of this minimal Hamiltonian highlights that significant aspects of linguistic processing can be effectively modeled using pairwise semantic interactions.

These findings reinforce the conceptual bridge between condensed-matter physics and mechanistic interpretability, translating complex attention mechanisms into accessible frameworks of effective fields, order parameters, and interaction-driven dynamics. This perspective opens possibilities for targeted interventions in model behavior, including precise edits, bias audits, and enhanced robustness. Furthermore, the outlined stochastic Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert approach offers a physically informed alternative for text generation, incorporating precession and damping dynamics into diffusion-based sampling. Thus, the spin–bath formalism not only elucidates current Transformer operations but also hints at huge possibilities for future progress in physics-inspired language modeling.
